course.title: Cognitive Psychology
course.description: Cognitive psychology is the scientific study of mental processes such as perception, attention, memory, language, reasoning, and decision making. This course treats the mind as an information processor and follows the field from the cognitive revolution to modern experiments on memory, bias, and thought. Its structure is informed by the entry on cognitive psychology from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: The cognitive revolution challenged which previously dominant approach?
questions.explanation: It rejected behaviorism's refusal to study the internal mental processes between stimulus and response.

questions.prompt: The cocktail-party effect describes...
options: following one conversation while tuning out others, yet still catching your own name
questions.explanation: Selective attention filters input, but a salient signal like your name can break through from an unattended channel.

questions.prompt: In the multi-store model, information usually flows...
options: into all three stores at once
questions.explanation: Sensory memory feeds short-term memory, which, with rehearsal, feeds long-term memory.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many items can short-term memory hold at once?
questions.explanation: Miller's 'magical number seven, plus or minus two.'

questions.prompt: A memory that exists but cannot be recalled without the right cue is a failure of...
questions.explanation: Cue-dependent forgetting is a retrieval failure - the trace is present but inaccessible.

questions.prompt: Elizabeth Loftus is best known for research on...
options: the misinformation effect and eyewitness memory
questions.explanation: She showed that leading questions can distort what witnesses remember.

questions.prompt: A schema is best described as...
options: a structured set of expectations about a situation
questions.explanation: Schemas package what we expect about a situation, speeding understanding but biasing memory.

questions.prompt: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind is the...
questions.explanation: The availability heuristic, described by Kahneman and Tversky.

lessons.title: The cognitive revolution and the mind as information processor
lessons.grammar_note: The processor metaphor is a model, not a literal claim - the mind resembles an information processor, it is not identical to one.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the cognitive revolution replaced, describe the mind-as-information-processor metaphor, and name the main research methods cognitive scientists use. Warm-up: before you read on, why might watching only outward behavior fail to explain how someone solves a puzzle in their head?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For the first half of the twentieth century, behaviorism dominated psychology and treated the mind as a black box - only observable stimuli and responses counted as evidence. The cognitive revolution of the 1950s and 1960s argued that the internal steps between stimulus and response are real and can be studied rigorously. Researchers borrowed a powerful metaphor from computing: the mind takes in information, encodes it, transforms it, stores it, and retrieves it, much like a processor running operations on data. This framing let psychologists ask precise questions about capacity, speed, and the order of mental operations. Cognition became the study of how information flows through a limited system. The metaphor is a tool for generating testable predictions, not a literal claim that brains are machines, and careful researchers keep that distinction in view.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: George Miller's 1956 paper on the 'magical number seven, plus or minus two' showed that short-term memory has a measurable limit and helped launch the field. Ulric Neisser named the discipline in his 1967 book Cognitive Psychology. Noam Chomsky's critique of behaviorist accounts of language pushed many scientists toward mental structure. Herbert Simon and Allen Newell modeled human thinking as step-by-step information processing. Donald Broadbent carried the information metaphor into the study of attention, giving the new approach early, concrete results.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What did behaviorism refuse to study? 2) Name one thing the processor metaphor lets you measure. 3) Who named the field in 1967? 4) What is a reaction-time study good for? 5) Is the mind literally a computer? Answers: 1) internal mental processes - the contents of the black box. 2) capacity, speed, or the order of mental operations. 3) Ulric Neisser. 4) inferring the number or duration of hidden mental steps between stimulus and response. 5) No - it is a useful metaphor, not a literal equation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking cognitive psychology throws out behavior as data - it still measures behavior carefully, then reasons back to the mental steps that produced it. Mistake: taking the processor metaphor literally. The methods of the field include controlled experiments, reaction-time measurement, systematic error analysis, and, more recently, brain imaging. Exit: (a) In which decade did the cognitive revolution take hold? (b) Name one research method cognitive psychologists use. Answers: the 1950s and 1960s; controlled experiments, reaction-time studies, error analysis, or brain imaging.

lessons.title: Perception and attention
lessons.grammar_note: Sensation is the raw signal; perception is the brain's interpretation of it - keep the two words distinct.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish sensation from perception, explain selective attention, and describe the cocktail-party effect. Warm-up: in a noisy room full of chatter, how do you still manage to catch your own name across the crowd?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sensation is the raw signal your senses detect; perception is the brain's interpretation of that signal into objects, scenes, and meaning. Because the world sends far more information than the mind can fully process, attention acts as a filter that selects what receives deeper processing. Selective attention is the ability to focus on one stream of input while ignoring others. The classic demonstration is the cocktail-party effect: at a crowded party you can follow one conversation and tune out the rest, yet a salient signal such as your own name can break through from a channel you were ignoring. This tells us the filter is not a hard on-off gate - unattended information is still monitored at a shallow level. Attention is limited, and whatever falls outside it can be missed entirely, as studies of inattentional blindness show.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Colin Cherry studied the cocktail-party problem using dichotic listening, playing different messages to each ear. Donald Broadbent proposed an early filter model in which attention blocks unattended input early in processing. Anne Treisman revised this with attenuation theory, arguing that the filter turns down rather than fully blocks unattended channels - which explains why your name still gets through. Later work on inattentional blindness by Simons and Chabris showed that people can miss an obvious event while their attention is focused elsewhere.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the difference between sensation and perception? 2) What does selective attention do? 3) Name the effect where your name cuts through background chatter. 4) Whose attenuation theory softened the early filter model? 5) What does inattentional blindness show? Answers: 1) sensation is the raw signal, perception is its interpretation. 2) it focuses processing on one input while ignoring others. 3) the cocktail-party effect. 4) Anne Treisman. 5) that focused attention can cause us to miss obvious unattended events.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming we perceive everything in front of us - attention is a bottleneck, and much is filtered out before it reaches awareness. Mistake: treating the attention filter as a perfect switch; unattended input is attenuated, not erased. Exit: (a) Which comes first, sensation or perception? (b) Why can your own name break through a conversation you are ignoring? Answers: sensation comes first, then perception interprets it; because unattended channels are still monitored at a shallow level, so a highly salient signal can get through.

lessons.title: Memory systems: the multi-store model
lessons.grammar_note: Short-term memory holds information briefly; working memory holds and actively manipulates it - the newer model adds the manipulation.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the sensory, short-term, and long-term stores, explain working memory, and state the rough capacity limits of each. Warm-up: how many random digits do you think you could repeat back correctly after hearing them just once?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The multi-store model, proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin, splits memory into three stores. Sensory memory holds a very brief, high-capacity snapshot of incoming sensation - a visual trace lasts around half a second. Attention transfers some of this into short-term memory, a limited store that holds roughly seven items for a few seconds unless they are rehearsed. Rehearsal and deeper encoding move information into long-term memory, a vast and durable store. Later, Baddeley and Hitch replaced the passive short-term box with working memory, an active system that both holds and manipulates information. Working memory includes a phonological loop for sound-based material, a visuospatial sketchpad for images and space, and a central executive that directs attention between them. The upgrade matters because we do not merely store information briefly - we work on it.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin introduced the multi-store model in 1968. George Miller's 'magical number seven, plus or minus two' set the classic estimate of short-term capacity. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed the working-memory model in 1974, adding the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and the central executive. Baddeley later added the episodic buffer, a component that binds information together across the subsystems and links it to long-term memory.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which store holds a brief sensory snapshot? 2) Roughly how many items fit in short-term memory? 3) What moves information into long-term memory? 4) Name the two slave systems of working memory. 5) What does the central executive do? Answers: 1) sensory memory. 2) about seven, plus or minus two. 3) rehearsal and deeper, meaningful encoding. 4) the phonological loop and the visuospatial sketchpad. 5) it directs and allocates attention between the subsystems.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing short-term memory with working memory - working memory also manipulates information, it does not just hold it. Mistake: thinking long-term memory has a known capacity limit; for practical purposes it is effectively vast. Exit: (a) Who proposed the multi-store model? (b) What is the central executive's job? Answers: Atkinson and Shiffrin; to control attention and coordinate the working-memory subsystems.

questions.prompt: The mind-as-information-processor metaphor compares the mind to...
questions.explanation: The mind encodes, stores, transforms, and retrieves information much like a processor.

questions.prompt: Who named the field in the 1967 book Cognitive Psychology?
questions.explanation: Neisser's 1967 book gave the discipline its name.

questions.prompt: Treisman's attenuation theory says that unattended channels are...
questions.explanation: Attenuation, not full blocking, explains why your own name still gets through.

questions.prompt: Which store holds a brief, high-capacity snapshot of raw sensation?
questions.explanation: Sensory memory lasts a fraction of a second before attention selects from it.

questions.prompt: In Baddeley and Hitch's model, sound-based material is held by the...
questions.explanation: The phonological loop handles verbal and acoustic information.

questions.prompt: The central executive's main job is to...
questions.explanation: It coordinates the working-memory subsystems and controls attention.

lessons.title: Encoding, forgetting, and false memory
lessons.grammar_note: Memory is reconstructive, not a recording - each retrieval rebuilds the event, so it can be edited.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Separate encoding, storage, and retrieval; explain why we forget; and describe how memory can be distorted, including eyewitness errors. Warm-up: is forgetting always a failure to store something, or can it be a failure to find what is still there?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Memory has three phases: encoding (getting information in), storage (holding it over time), and retrieval (getting it back out). Failures can happen at any of them. Encoding that connects new material to existing knowledge - deep, meaningful processing - produces far better recall than shallow rote repetition. Forgetting has several causes: traces may fade, competing memories may interfere, or the right retrieval cue may simply be missing, so the memory is present but inaccessible. Crucially, memory is reconstructive, not a faithful recording. Each time we retrieve an event, we rebuild it from fragments plus expectations, which means memory can be edited in the process. This leaves it open to distortion, and false memories - confident recollections of things that never happened - can be created, especially when misleading information is introduced after the event.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Hermann Ebbinghaus charted the forgetting curve, showing rapid early loss that then levels off. Frederic Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study showed that recall is reconstructive and shaped by schemas. Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated the misinformation effect: leading questions change what witnesses report. In one study, asking how fast cars were going when they 'smashed' rather than 'hit' raised speed estimates and led people to recall broken glass that was never there. Her work reshaped how courts weigh eyewitness testimony.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three memory phases. 2) Give one cause of forgetting that is not fading. 3) What kind of encoding aids recall? 4) What is the misinformation effect? 5) Who showed that leading questions alter eyewitness reports? Answers: 1) encoding, storage, and retrieval. 2) interference, or a missing retrieval cue. 3) deep, meaningful processing that links new material to prior knowledge. 4) misleading information given after an event distorts the memory of that event. 5) Elizabeth Loftus.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating memory as a faithful video recording - it is reconstructed at each retrieval and can be edited. Mistake: assuming a confident eyewitness is an accurate one; confidence and accuracy can come apart. Exit: (a) Which phase fails when a memory exists but you cannot find it? (b) What did Loftus's 'smashed versus hit' study reveal? Answers: retrieval (a cue-dependent failure); that wording after an event can inflate estimates and plant details that were never present.

lessons.title: Concepts, schemas, language and thought
lessons.grammar_note: Category membership is usually graded around a prototype, not an all-or-nothing matter of rigid rules.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how concepts and schemas organize knowledge, and weigh the claim that language shapes thought. Warm-up: what mental 'folder' do you open the moment someone says the word restaurant?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Knowledge is organized, not a loose heap of facts. Concepts are mental categories that group things by shared features, letting us treat a new item as a member of a known class. Rather than a strict checklist of rules, many concepts cluster around a prototype, the most typical example, so a robin feels more bird-like than a penguin does. Schemas are larger knowledge structures that package what we expect about a situation - a restaurant schema includes being seated, ordering, eating, and paying. Schemas speed understanding but can also bias memory toward the expected. Language interacts with all of this. The strong claim that language fully determines thought is doubted, but a weaker version - that the words and categories a language offers can nudge attention and memory - has experimental support.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Eleanor Rosch developed prototype theory, showing that category membership is graded around typical examples. Frederic Bartlett introduced schemas to explain reconstructive memory. Benjamin Lee Whorf and Edward Sapir are linked to linguistic relativity, the idea that language shapes thought. Noam Chomsky argued instead for a universal grammar underlying all human languages, pushing back on strong relativity. Roger Brown and others tested how color naming and categories vary across languages, giving the debate concrete data.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a concept? 2) What is a prototype? 3) What does a restaurant schema help you do? 4) State the weak version of linguistic relativity. 5) Who proposed prototype theory? Answers: 1) a mental category that groups items by shared features. 2) the most typical example of a category. 3) anticipate the usual sequence of events, speeding comprehension. 4) language can influence, but not fully determine, attention and memory. 5) Eleanor Rosch.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking categories have rigid, all-or-nothing boundaries; membership is often graded around a prototype. Mistake: accepting the strong claim that language fully determines thought - the evidence supports only a weaker influence. Exit: (a) What is a schema? (b) Which is better supported, strong or weak linguistic relativity? Answers: a structured packet of expectations about a situation or object; the weak version.

items.translation: the process of converting incoming information into a form that memory can store
items.example: Linking a new name to a vivid image is a form of deep encoding.

items.translation: the process of getting stored information back out of memory
items.example: A good cue can trigger retrieval of a fact that felt forgotten.

items.translation: an active system that briefly holds and manipulates information
items.example: You use working memory to add two numbers in your head.

items.translation: focusing processing on one input while ignoring competing streams
items.example: Selective attention lets you read in a noisy cafe.

items.translation: a structured packet of expectations about a situation or object
items.example: Your classroom schema tells you where to sit and when to speak.

items.translation: a fast mental shortcut that usually works but can fail
items.example: Judging a word's frequency by how easily it comes to mind is a heuristic.

items.translation: the most typical example of a category, which membership is judged against
items.example: A sparrow is closer to the bird prototype than an ostrich is.

items.translation: distortion of a memory by misleading information given after the event
items.example: A leading question produced the misinformation effect in Loftus's studies.

questions.prompt: The three phases of memory, in order, are...
questions.explanation: Information is encoded, stored over time, and later retrieved.

questions.prompt: In Loftus's study, asking if cars 'smashed' rather than 'hit' led witnesses to...
options: give higher speed estimates and recall glass that was not there
questions.explanation: Post-event wording distorted the memory - the misinformation effect.

questions.prompt: Deep, meaningful encoding improves recall more than...
questions.explanation: Processing meaning produces more durable memories than shallow repetition does.

questions.prompt: A robin feels more 'bird-like' than a penguin because of...
questions.explanation: Category membership is graded around a prototype, the most typical example.

questions.prompt: A restaurant schema mainly helps you...
options: anticipate the usual sequence of events
questions.explanation: Schemas package expected sequences, speeding comprehension.

questions.prompt: The better-supported version of linguistic relativity holds that language...
options: has no effect on thought at all
questions.explanation: The weak version - language nudges rather than dictates - has experimental support.

lessons.title: Problem solving, reasoning, and decision making
lessons.grammar_note: An algorithm guarantees a correct answer but can be slow; a heuristic is a fast shortcut that can fail in predictable ways.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe problem-solving strategies, tell algorithms from heuristics, and name common biases that skew reasoning and decisions. Warm-up: when you decide a restaurant must be good because it is crowded, what shortcut are you leaning on?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Problem solving moves from an initial state to a goal state. An algorithm is a step-by-step method that guarantees a solution but can be slow; a heuristic is a fast shortcut that usually works but sometimes fails. Means-end analysis reduces the gap between where you are and the goal one step at a time. Reasoning and decision making lean on heuristics too. The availability heuristic judges likelihood by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid events feel more common than they are. The representativeness heuristic judges membership by similarity to a stereotype, ignoring base rates. Framing shows that how a choice is worded - as a gain or as a loss - changes what people pick, even when the options are identical. These shortcuts are efficient, but they produce systematic, predictable errors called biases.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky mapped the heuristics-and-biases program in the 1970s, describing availability, representativeness, and anchoring. Their prospect theory showed that people weigh losses more heavily than equal gains. Kahneman later contrasted fast, intuitive thinking with slow, effortful thinking. Herbert Simon introduced bounded rationality and satisficing - choosing an option that is good enough rather than searching for the optimal one. Peter Wason's selection task exposed systematic errors in everyday logical reasoning.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How does an algorithm differ from a heuristic? 2) What does the availability heuristic use to judge likelihood? 3) What does the representativeness heuristic ignore? 4) What is framing? 5) Who developed prospect theory? Answers: 1) an algorithm guarantees a solution but is slow, while a heuristic is a fast shortcut that can fail. 2) how easily relevant examples come to mind. 3) base rates. 4) how a choice is worded as a gain or a loss changes the decision. 5) Kahneman and Tversky.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating heuristics as simply irrational - they are efficient shortcuts that fail in predictable ways. Mistake: assuming people weigh gains and losses equally; losses usually loom larger. Studying these effects relies on the field's research methods: controlled experiments, reaction-time data, and systematic analysis of the errors people make. Exit: (a) Name one heuristic described by Kahneman and Tversky. (b) What is satisficing? Answers: availability, representativeness, or anchoring; choosing the first option that is good enough rather than searching for the optimal one.
